That team reports Muon lost to SGD at every size, which conflicts with E006. The PR and its repo now return 404, so I only saw it through search snippets. The finding most likely to matter is in the reference code, on weight decay. In airbench94_muon, Muon filters get no weight decay at all. They are instead renormalised to a fixed norm before every update. Weight decay goes only to the whitening bias, the BN biases and the head, as weight_decay=wd/lr, with wd=2e-6×batch. Hiverge's faster CIFAR-10 record uses wd≈1.6e-3, about 0.4× airbench94_muon's 4e-3, and also LS 0.09, BN momentum 0.557 and SiLU. structured_output.summary:
I found no public CIFAR-100 recipe faster than the current tip, E016 (6.58 s at 0.7607). The best public one is abdullah-athar PR #3: 8.11 s and 75.29% over 40 seeds, using SGD at 8.5 epochs with widths 128/384/576 and LS 0.3. That team reports Muon lost to SGD at every size, which conflicts with E006. The PR and its repo now return 404, so I only saw it through search snippets. The organiser repos list only the 59.3 s ResNet9 baseline and no leaderboard. The Fable/fulcrum write-up covers CIFAR-10 only.

The finding most likely to matter is in the reference code, on weight decay. In airbench94_muon, Muon filters get no weight decay at all. They are instead renormalised to a fixed norm before every update. Weight decay goes only to the whitening bias, the BN biases and the head, as weight_decay=wd/lr, with wd=2e-6×batch. Hiverge's faster CIFAR-10 record uses wd≈1.6e-3, about 0.4× airbench94_muon's 4e-3, and also LS 0.09, BN momentum 0.557 and SiLU. Two things follow, depending on whether the arena port renormalises its filters (the brief doesn't say):
- If it does, E016's wd halving can only have acted through the SGD groups, and the next grid points should target BN-bias and head wd (×0.25, 0).
- If it doesn't, adding renormalisation and removing filter wd is an untested lever.

Hiverge also renormalises less often as training goes on (every 2 steps early, every 17 late), which saves a little per-step overhead. It also bakes in values not yet tried here: bias LR decayed to 0 within 3 epochs, a separate head LR, brightness/contrast jitter, and SiLU.

The airbench paper's ablations bear on four hypotheses:
- **Alternating flip (H1.4/H1.4.1):** worth 15% in epochs at 10 epochs without TTA, but only 3.8% when Cutout is also used.
- **Whitening and Dirac init (H1.1.2):** frozen patch-whitening cut epochs-to-94% from 45 to 21, and Dirac init from 21 to 18.
- **Lookahead:** saved 1.5 epochs.
- **TTA:** multi-crop TTA was worth 6.6 epochs on CIFAR-10. It is banned here, which explains why this task needs more epochs than the CIFAR-10 references.

airbench96_faster's Lookahead keeps an average of the full state_dict, including BN running buffers, and resets the fast weights to that average on every update. So the BN statistics already roughly match the averaged weights, and BN recalibration (H1.3.6) should gain little. The proxy-model data filtering (H2.4) comes only bundled with other changes, in a 45-epoch run, so there is no isolated evidence for it at about 9 epochs.

The airbench scripts all run at about 110-116 TFLOP/s on an A100. The arena's 32 px epoch time (0.89 s) fits that rate, so remaining systems gains would have to come from beating cuDNN or from overhead that is already near zero, which backs E011/E015. Jordan's "Calibrated Chaos" paper says seed-to-seed spread is mostly finite-test-set noise, which fits the 0.24 pp per-seed std (H4.1).

findings.claim: In the reference Muon recipe, Muon gives no weight decay to the conv filters. Instead, each step renormalises every filter tensor to a fixed norm (p.data.mul_(len(p.data)**0.5 / p.data.norm())) before the Newton-Schulz update. Weight decay goes only to three SGD groups: the whitening bias (lr 0.053), the BN biases (lr 0.053) and the head (lr 0.67). Each group uses weight_decay=wd/lr with wd=2e-6*batch_size (0.004 at batch 2000). The whitening bias LR decays to 0 over the first 3 epochs; everything else decays linearly to 0 over 8 epochs. Other settings: LS 0.2, SGD momentum 0.85, Muon momentum 0.6, frozen BN weights, BN momentum 0.6 (passed to torch as 0.4).
findings.relevance: E016 halved wd 'for all groups including Muon filters'. If the arena port renormalises filters like the reference does, filter wd does nothing and the whole E016 gain came from the BN-bias and head groups. If it doesn't renormalise, filter-norm control is an untested difference from the reference. Either way, the next wd grid points should be set separately for the BN-bias/head groups (×0.25, 0) and the filter group.

findings.claim: The Hiverge CIFAR-10 record (1.98 s to 94%) retunes airbench94_muon to: batch 1536, 7.65 epochs, Muon lr 0.205 with momentum 0.655, bias lr 0.0573, head lr 0.5415, SGD momentum 0.825, and wd=1.0418e-6*1536≈1.6e-3 (about 0.4× airbench94_muon's 4e-3), applied multiplicatively to the filters as well. Other settings: LS 0.09, BN momentum 0.5566 with eps 1e-12 and frozen BN weights, SiLU instead of GELU, and brightness ±0.14 / contrast ±0.13 jitter. Filter renormalisation runs only every norm_freq steps, rising from 2 to 17 over training. Whitening uses SVD on 960 images. There is no EMA.
findings.relevance: This is independent evidence that tuned wd sits well below the airbench default, which fits E016 and suggests trying wd ×0.25–0.4. Doing the filter renorm only every k steps cuts per-step optimizer overhead with no accuracy loss reported. SiLU, colour jitter and a lower SGD momentum are untested axes.

findings.claim: The best public CIFAR-100 speedrun result I found is 75.29% mean (std 0.25 pp over 40 seeds) in 8.11 s (std 0.02 s) on an A100-SXM4-80GB. The recipe is an airbench-style net with 3-conv groups at widths 128/384/576, LS 0.3, lr 9.0, wd 0.012 and 8.5 epochs. LS 0.3 beat both 0.2 and 0.4 there, and Muon lost to SGD at every width, so it was dropped.
findings.relevance: The current tip (6.58 s) already beats this public mark by about 20%. Their Muon result conflicts with E006 (+0.66 pp), possibly because their Muon was untuned or had no EMA. Their LS result conflicts with E013, where LS 0.2 vs 0.3 was flat with EMA on, which suggests EMA flattens the LS optimum. Their 40-seed std of 0.25 pp matches E012's 0.24 pp.

findings.claim: Alternating flip vs random flip on airbench94 without TTA or Cutout saves 15.0% of epochs at 10 epochs, 27.1% at 20 and 38.3% at 40. With TTA the saving is 5.3% at 10 epochs. With Cutout it is 3.84% without TTA and 1.13% with. Frozen patch-whitening cut epochs-to-94% from 45 to 21, Dirac init from 21 to 18, and Lookahead from 13.5 to 12.0. Multi-crop TTA was worth 6.6 epochs (10.8→4.2). airbench96 reaches 79.27% on CIFAR-100 without Cutout. BN biases train at 64× the LR, with frozen BN scales.
findings.relevance: Supports H1.4/H1.4.1: with TTA banned and no Cutout, alternating flip should be worth about 15% of epochs at around 9 epochs, which is roughly 0.3–0.5 pp. It also supports H1.1.2: whitening plus Dirac init roughly halve epochs on CIFAR-10. The banned TTA is worth several epochs, which explains why 9 epochs are needed here versus about 8 for CIFAR-10 at 94%.

findings.claim: LookaheadState keeps a copy of the full net.state_dict(), BN running_mean/var included. Every 5 steps it lerps toward the current weights with decay=0.95**5*(step/total)**3, then copies the average back into the net, which resets the fast weights. The final update(decay=1.0) leaves the net equal to the average. Weight decay for the BN biases is divided by bias_scaler (64), so the effective decay matches the other params. Data filtering uses a proxy net at widths 32/64/64 and depth 2, keeps the top-loss 512 of each 1024 batch, and runs inside a 45-epoch schedule. Hyperparameters: lr 9.0, momentum 0.85, wd 0.012, LS 0.2, whiten-bias training for 3 epochs.
findings.relevance: Because the BN buffers are averaged and the fast weights are reset to the average, the BN statistics already roughly match the final weights, so BN recalibration (H1.3.6) should gain little. A plain EMA with no reset (H1.3.5) would leave the BN buffers out of step with the weights more than Lookahead does. The data filtering has no isolated ablation and was only shown in a 45-epoch regime, so H2.4 stays weakly supported for 9-epoch runs. The E016 post-mortem assumes BN-bias decay is amplified 64×; that is only true if the port does not divide wd by bias_scaler, so the code should be checked.

findings.claim: Published compute and time: airbench94_muon 0.29 PFLOPs in 2.59 s; airbench94_compiled 0.36 PF in 3.09 s; airbench96 4.9 PF in 34.7 s; airbench96_faster 3.1 PF in 27.3 s, after adding data filtering and a narrower last group. All of these run at about 110–116 TFLOP/s on an A100, roughly 35–37% of fp16 peak.
findings.relevance: The arena's 32 px epoch (0.89 s with widths 128/384/512) is consistent with this throughput, so the compiled net is already at reference efficiency. Further systems gains (H2.2.x, H2.2.3) would have to come from beating cuDNN conv efficiency, not from Python overhead. This fits E011's estimate of ~5% fixed overhead and E015's <1% gain.

findings.claim: Test-set accuracy varies a lot between seeds (seeds can differ by 1.3% on CIFAR-10), but variance on the underlying test distribution is tiny (e.g. 0.033% std for 64-epoch CIFAR-10). An independent-errors model (finite test-set sampling) reproduces the observed spread.
findings.relevance: Per-seed std of about 0.24 pp on a 10k-image test set at p≈0.755 is mostly finite-sample noise that every recipe shares. The 3-seed mean SE of about 0.14 pp is therefore close to an irreducible floor. Differences under about 0.3 pp cannot be resolved with 3 seeds, but a recipe's 40-seed mean should sit close to its expected accuracy. This supports H4.1 and H4.1.2.

findings.claim: The EMA-dynamics paper finds EMA needs less LR decay than last-iterate SGD because averaging already reduces noise, and that BN statistics, not the parameters, are what break an EMA model at long averaging windows (recomputing BN stats recovers full performance). SWA needs a BN recompute pass because it averages weights only.
findings.relevance: This explains E009: with Lookahead/EMA on, an LR floor of 0.07 vs 0 made no difference. It also implies BN recalibration helps only if the averaged model's BN buffers are stale. airbench-style Lookahead averages those buffers, so expect a small gain for H1.3.6 unless the EMA window is made longer.

findings.claim: Fable's CIFAR-10 record (1.828 s vs Hiverge's 1.978 s, a 7.6% legitimate gain) came mainly from progressive resizing (24→28→32 px), with schedule compression from 10.5 to 9.0–9.75 epochs, CUDA-graph/optimizer fusion, pooling tweaks and minor hyperparameter tuning. About 0.15 s of the measured gain was spec gaming: augmentation precomputed outside the timed region, a machine lottery, and thermal cooldowns. Hiverge's gains came from a vectorised Muon, vectorised crop plus colour jitter, a compiled step, SiLU, SVD whitening and retuning; per-technique numbers are not given.
findings.relevance: Progressive resizing is the leading lever in both the CIFAR-10 and arena results (E007). The CIFAR-10 record also relies on a lengthened schedule, which fits E011's finding that coarse resolutions hit a cliff. Neither write-up has CIFAR-100 data. Precomputing augmentation outside the timed region would break this task's rules and must be avoided.
